## Instrument Families and Special Cases {#sec-instrument-families}

The preceding sections developed what an instrument has to do: shift the treatment, stay out of
the outcome equation, and move everyone in the same direction. Those are properties of a
research design, not of a variable, and they are argued rather than tested. What follows is the
catalogue.

Table \@ref(tab:iv-workhorse-instruments) sketched the workhorse families in a single row each.
The sections below take the families that carry the most weight in current applied work and
develop each one properly: how the instrument is constructed, what identification argument it
rests on, which diagnostics a referee will expect, and where the design has been shown to break.

They fall into four groups. The first borrows variation from an institution that assigns
something as if at random: shift-share and recentered designs
(Sections \@ref(sec-shift-share-iv) and \@ref(sec-recentered-iv)), decision-maker leniency
(Section \@ref(sec-examiner-design)), quasi-random advertising timing
(Section \@ref(sec-single-source-tv-iv)), and the statutory rules behind simulated instruments
(Section \@ref(sec-simulated-iv)). The second borrows it from the physical or social world:
geographic proximity (Section \@ref(sec-distance-iv)), weather and wind
(Section \@ref(sec-weather-iv)), genetic variants (Section \@ref(sec-mendelian-randomization)),
and network position (Section \@ref(sec-network-peer-iv)). The third manufactures instruments
internally, out of the data's own structure rather than from outside it: lagged levels in a
dynamic panel (Section \@ref(sec-dynamic-panel-iv)) and higher moments of a mismeasured
regressor (Section \@ref(sec-higher-moment-iv)), both of which trade an external variation
argument for a distributional assumption. The fourth deals with cases that are less about
finding an instrument than about what to do when the usual machinery does not apply: proxy
variables (Section \@ref(sec-proxy-variables)), where no instrument exists but a stand-in for
the confounder does, and binary endogenous regressors
(Section \@ref(sec-binary-endogenous-regressors)), where the linear model itself is the problem.
Section \@ref(sec-finance-shock-iv) collects the constructions specific to corporate finance,
which cut across the first three groups.

A theme recurs often enough to state in advance. In several of these families the first-stage
statistic is uninformative about validity, and in two of them it is actively misleading, large
precisely when the identifying assumption fails. Strength and validity are separate questions,
and only one of them has a test.

The sections are independent of one another. A reader working on a specific design can go
directly to it.
